headline: P0041 (Family Practice, GA): 99215 share of 20.8% vs 2.5% expected, concentrated on patients with 0-1 chronic conditions; pattern consistent with upcoding
rationale: P0041 billed 99215 on 52 of 250 claims (20.8%), while the expected share given patient complexity is 2.5% (z vs peers 2.35, risk-adjusted score 6.73). The excess is not explained by a sicker panel. Most visits are with low-complexity patients: 177 of 250 are with patients who have 0-1 chronic conditions, and 36 of the 52 99215s fall there. That is a 16.3% share for 0-condition patients against 2.1% for all providers, and 24.7% against 3.4% for 1-condition patients. The sampled 99215s on 0-condition patients carry single routine diagnoses, such as a follow-up exam (Z09: C0020325, C0020404), low back pain (M54.50: C0020348, C0020364, C0020470), UTI (N39.0: C0020339, C0020443, C0020515), rash (R21: C0020384, C0020410, C0020497) and abdominal pain (R10.9: C0020335, C0020521). On their face, these do not suggest high-complexity decision-making. The provider also bills well above expected on 2-3 condition patients. High-level billing on 4+ condition patients (e.g., C0020426, C0020473 for a 96-year-old with 6 conditions, C0020489) is plausible, but those are only 5 visits. The packet has no clinical documentation, time or MDM data, and the claim lists are samples, so this is a pattern to verify, not a finding.
next_steps: Request medical records for the sampled 99215 claims on 0-1 condition patients (e.g., C0020325, C0020348, C0020384, C0020443) and check whether documented MDM or total time supports level 5.
Pull a larger or complete sample of 99215 claims to confirm the low-complexity concentration seen in the tables.
Review the 99214 billing too: 146 of 250 claims (58%) are 99214, which may point to broader level inflation (e.g., C0020413, a 99214 for low back pain in a 0-condition patient).
Check whether diagnosis coding understates patient acuity (missing chronic condition codes) before concluding the panel is low complexity.
Compare against the provider's 2024 visit timing and volume per day to test whether time-based 99215 billing is feasible.
